date.note: The Spanish original, Teologia de la liberacion: Perspectivas, was published at Lima (CEP) in 1971, developing a 1968 lecture by Gustavo Gutierrez. The standard English translation, A Theology of Liberation: History, Politics, and Salvation, translated and edited by Sister Caridad Inda and John Eagleson, was published by Orbis Books (Maryknoll, NY) in 1973; a revised edition with a new introduction appeared in 1988. The year 1971 marks the first Spanish edition.

summary: A Theology of Liberation (Teologia de la liberacion, 1971; English, Orbis, 1973) is the book by the Peruvian Dominican priest Gustavo Gutierrez that is widely regarded as the founding programmatic text of Latin American liberation theology. It frames theology, on Gutierrez's account, as 'critical reflection on Christian praxis in the light of the word of God', centers the 'preferential option for the poor', and understands liberation from social, political, and economic injustice as included within, though not reducing, the one saving work of Christ.
description:
A Theology of Liberation is the best-known work of Gustavo Gutierrez (1928-2024), the Peruvian Dominican priest and theologian regarded on the standard account of the movement's historians as the principal founder of Latin American liberation theology. It grew out of a 1968 lecture and was published in Spanish as Teologia de la liberacion: Perspectivas (Lima: CEP, 1971); the standard English translation, A Theology of Liberation: History, Politics, and Salvation, translated and edited by Sister Caridad Inda and John Eagleson, was issued by Orbis Books in 1973, with a revised edition carrying a new introduction in 1988. It is commonly treated in the scholarship as the text that gave the movement its programmatic name and statement.

On Gutierrez's own account the book redefines the theological task itself. Rather than treating theology primarily as a body of doctrine or as rational wisdom, he presents it as 'critical reflection on Christian praxis in the light of the word of God', that is, reflection that begins from committed Christian action on behalf of the poor and returns to that action to purify and direct it. This ordering, praxis first and theological reflection as a second act, is stated by the movement as one of its defining methodological claims. Bound to it is the commitment for which the book is most widely known, the 'preferential option for the poor': reading the gospel from the standpoint of the poor and the oppressed and making their liberation a first concern of Christian life and reflection. Gutierrez sets this commitment in the Latin American ecclesial context of the 1968 Medellin conference of the Latin American bishops (CELAM), which applied the Second Vatican Council to the continent.

A further distinctive move of the book is its account of liberation and salvation. Gutierrez holds, on his own account, that salvation is not reduced to social, political, or economic liberation but includes it: he distinguishes levels or dimensions of liberation, from unjust social structures, from everything that dehumanizes, and from sin as the ultimate root, while insisting that these are bound together within the single saving work of Christ. To analyze the situation of poverty and oppression the book draws on social-scientific tools, including categories associated with Marxist social analysis such as class and structural injustice; on the movement's own account this is employed as a tool of social analysis rather than as an adoption of Marxist philosophy or atheism. This entry attributes these positions (theology as critical reflection on praxis, the preferential option for the poor, and liberation as integral to but not exhaustive of salvation) to Gutierrez and to the work, and records the work's standing as the founding text of liberation theology as a matter of scholarly report, without endorsing or adjudicating its claims. The book was engaged, and in part critiqued, by the Roman Catholic magisterium, whose 1984 and 1986 CDF Instructions on liberation theology are recorded elsewhere in the dataset as attributed positions; this entry does not adjudicate that reception.
editorial_notes:
This entry describes A Theology of Liberation on Christian terms (neutrality #1, #4, #6) and attributes its theological claims to Gustavo Gutierrez and to the work itself. Gutierrez's definition of theology as 'critical reflection on Christian praxis in the light of the word of God', the preferential option for the poor, and the account of liberation as included within but not reducing salvation are stated as his and the movement's attributed positions, not endorsed or adjudicated; the work's standing as the founding text of liberation theology is reported as scholarly assessment, not as the editor's verdict.
